newsitem.title: USA: NASD bars 12 brokers for life.
newsitem.headline: NASD bars 12 brokers for life.

text.p: The regulatory arm of the National Association of Securities Dealers said Tuesday it barred for life 12 securities brokers suspected of paying stand-ins to take qualifying examinations.

NASD Regulation Inc. said the 12 were also fined amounts ranging from $25,000 to $50,000 each. It said its investigation is continuing and anticipates additional disciplinary actions will be completed shortly.

In announcing the action, NASD Regulation President Mary Schapiro president of NASD Regulation, said: "Violating the association's registration requirements, which exist to protect the public, is a serious offence, but paying someone to impersonate a candidate and take the examination for them is misconduct of the highest order."

NASD Regulation's sanctions stemmed from an investigation carried out by its New York district office, which disclosed the probe in early July. At the time, Martin Kuperberg, chief of the office, said "dozens" were under investigation and that one broker questioned had admitted paying a stand-in $2,500 to take the tests.

NASD Regulation oversees the nation's more than 510,000 securities industry registered representatives and 5,400 brokerage firms. The tests it administers are intended to insure that the candidate has a well-rounded knowledge of securities markets amd regulations. The goal is to assure the public that they are dealing with competent securities professionals.
The 12 brokers who agreed to the sanctions neither admitted nor denied any wrongdoing but waived their right to appeal, according to an NASD Regulation official in Washington.

The 12, who worked in New York area brokerages, were identified as Burton Butler Brous, Stephen Douglas Carollo, Peter Michael DelSeni, David Mark Gold, Kevin Michael Kelly, Frank Michael Mancini, Yury Moroz, Joseph John Pellegrino, Brian Thomas Rice, Peter Scali, Robert James Thornton and Felix Tkachenko.

NASD Regulation said that after the 12 were identified, each was summoned to answer questions regarding their suspected misconduct. Six refused to appear or answer questions, the regulatory arm said, but did not say who they were.
NASD Regulation rules require brokers to respond to an inquiry, and failure to do so is deemed a violation of its rules that carry sanctions, including a permanent bar from the industry, it said.
Schapiro said NASD Regulation will take all steps necessary to rid the industry of those who commit similar misconduct.
"Qualifying exams are securities professionals' first chance to prove themselves, and by cheating on the exams these individuals have proven beyond all doubt that they are not be trusted."
